entities.name: Richard Bassett
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Richard Bassett (1745–1815) was a Delaware lawyer, politician, and one of the Founding Fathers of the United States — a signer of the Constitution at the 1787 Philadelphia Convention, a Delaware delegate to the Constitutional Convention, the first Chief Justice of Delaware (1793–1799), Governor of Delaware (1799–1801), and a US Senator from Delaware (1789–1793). He was one of only a handful of men who signed the Constitution and subsequently held the full range of judicial, executive, and legislative office in the new government they had created.

Bassett's most remarkable personal transformation was his conversion to Methodism in the early 1780s under the influence of Francis Asbury — the itinerant Methodist bishop who was bringing the evangelical movement to the American frontier. Under Asbury's influence, Bassett became a Methodist of deep conviction and eventually an abolitionist — a striking evolution for a Delaware slaveholder who had signed a constitution that protected slavery. He freed his own enslaved people and became a supporter of manumission — an unusually progressive position for a prominent Federalist politician in a border state.

His conversion to Methodism also made him a patron of the early Methodist movement in America: he hosted Methodist gatherings at his Delaware estate and supported the institutional development of American Methodism in its formative decades.

Bassett's life illustrated the rare intersection of Founding-era constitutional authority with evangelical religious transformation and anti-slavery conviction.
